{{Short description|Branch of statistics mathematics}}
'''Functional data analysis''' (FDA) is a branch of [[statistics]] that analyses data providing information about curves, surfaces or anything else varying over a continuum.  In its most general form, under an FDA framework, each sample element of functional data is considered to be a random function. The physical continuum over which these functions are defined is often time, but may also be spatial location, wavelength, probability, etc. Intrinsically, functional data are infinite dimensional. The high intrinsic dimensionality of these data brings challenges for theory as well as computation, where these challenges vary with how the functional data were sampled. However, the high or infinite dimensional structure of the data is a rich source of information and there are many interesting challenges for research and data analysis.

==History==
Functional data analysis has roots going back to work by Grenander and Karhunen in the 1940s and 1950s.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Grenander|first=U.|date=1950|title=Stochastic processes and statistical inference|journal=Arkiv för Matematik|volume=1|issue=3|pages=195–277|doi=10.1007/BF02590638|bibcode=1950ArM.....1..195G|s2cid=120451372|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Rice|first1=JA|last2=Silverman|first2=BW.|date=1991|title=Estimating the mean and covariance structure nonparametrically when the data are curves|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society|volume=53|issue=1|pages=233–243|doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1991.tb01821.x }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Müller|first=HG.|date=2016|title=Peter Hall, functional data analysis and random objects|journal=Annals of Statistics|volume=44|issue=5|pages=1867–1887|doi=10.1214/16-AOS1492|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Karhunen|first=K|title=Zur Spektraltheorie stochastischer Prozesse|publisher=Annales Academiae scientiarum Fennicae|year=1946}}</ref> They considered the decomposition of square-integrable continuous time [[stochastic process]] into eigencomponents, now known as the [[Karhunen–Loève theorem|Karhunen-Loève decomposition]]. A rigorous analysis of [[functional principal components analysis]] was done in the 1970s by Kleffe, Dauxois and Pousse including results about the asymptotic distribution of the eigenvalues.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kleffe|first=J.|date=1973|title=Principal components of random variables with values in a seperable {{sic|hide=y}} HILBERT space|journal=Mathematische Operationsforschung und Statistik|volume=4|issue=5|pages=391–406|doi=10.1080/02331887308801137}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dauxois|first1=J|last2=Pousse|first2=A|last3=Romain|first3=Y.|date=1982|title=Asymptotic theory for the principal component analysis of a vector random function: Some applications to statistical inference|journal=Journal of Multivariate Analysis|volume=12|issue=1|pages=136–154|doi=10.1016/0047-259X(82)90088-4|doi-access=free}}</ref> More recently in the 1990s and 2000s the field has focused more on applications and understanding the effects of dense and sparse observations schemes. The term "Functional Data Analysis" was coined by [[James O. Ramsay]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite book|last1=Ramsay|first1=J|title=Functional Data Analysis, 2nd ed|last2=Silverman|first2=BW.|publisher=Springer|year=2005}}</ref>

==Mathematical formalism==
Random functions can be viewed as random elements taking values in a [[Hilbert space]], or as a [[stochastic process]].  The former is mathematically convenient, whereas the latter is somewhat more suitable from an applied perspective.  These two approaches coincide if the random functions are continuous and a condition called '''mean-squared continuity''' is satisfied.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Hsing|first1=T|title=Theoretical Foundations of Functional Data Analysis, with an Introduction to Linear Operators|last2=Eubank|first2=R|publisher=Wiley Series in Probability and Statistics|year=2015}}</ref>

===Hilbertian random variables===

In the Hilbert space viewpoint, one considers an <math>H</math>-valued random element <math>X</math>, where <math>H</math> is a separable Hilbert space such as the space of [[square-integrable function]]s <math>L^2[0,1]</math>.  Under the integrability condition that <math>\mathbb E\|X\|_{L^2}^2 = \mathbb{E} (\int^1_0 |X(t)|^2 dt) < \infty</math>, one can define the mean of <math>X</math> as the unique element <math>\mu\in H</math> satisfying
:  <math>
\mathbb E\langle X , h \rangle = \langle \mu,h\rangle ,\qquad h\in H.
</math>
This formulation is the [[Pettis integral]] but the mean can also be defined as [[Bochner integral]] <math>\mu=\mathbb EX</math>. Under the integrability condition that <math>\mathbb E\|X\|^2_{L^2}</math> is finite, the [[covariance operator]] of <math>X</math> is a [[linear operator]] <math>\mathcal{C}:H\to H</math> that is uniquely defined by the relation
: <math>
\mathcal{C} h = \mathbb E[\langle h,X-\mu\rangle (X-\mu)],\qquad h\in H,
</math>
or, in [[tensor product|tensor]] form, <math>\mathcal{C} = \mathbb E[(X-\mu)\otimes(X-\mu)]</math>.  The [[spectral theorem]] allows to decompose <math>X</math> as the [[Karhunen–Loève expansion|Karhunen-Loève decomposition]]
:  <math>
X=\mu+\sum_{i=1}^\infty \langle X,\varphi_i\rangle \varphi_i,
</math>
where <math>\varphi_i</math> are [[eigenvectors]] of <math>\mathcal C</math>, corresponding to the nonnegative [[eigenvalues]] of <math>\mathcal C</math>, in a non-increasing order.  Truncating this infinite series to a finite order underpins [[functional principal component analysis]].

===Stochastic processes===
The Hilbertian point of view is mathematically convenient, but abstract; the above considerations do not necessarily even view <math>X</math> as a function at all, since common choices of <math>H</math> like <math>L^2[0,1]</math> and [[Sobolev space]]s consist of equivalence classes, not functions.  The stochastic process perspective views <math>X</math> as a collection of random variables
:<math>
\{X(t)\}_{t\in [0,1]}
</math>
indexed by the unit interval (or more generally interval <math>\mathcal T</math>).  The mean and covariance functions are defined in a pointwise manner as
:<math>
\mu(t) = \mathbb EX(t),\qquad 
\Sigma(s,t) = \textrm{Cov}(X(s), X(t)),\qquad s,t\in [0, 1]
</math>
(if <math>\mathbb E[X(t)^2]<\infty</math> for all <math>t\in [0,1]</math>). 

Under the mean square continuity, <math>\mu</math> and <math>\Sigma</math> are continuous functions and then the covariance function <math>\Sigma</math> defines a covariance operator <math>\mathcal{C}:H\to H</math> given by 
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">(\mathcal{C} f)(t)
=\int_0^1 \Sigma(s,t)f(s) \, \mathrm{d}s.</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}} 

The [[spectral theorem]] applies to <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, yielding eigenpairs <math>(\lambda_j,\varphi_j)</math>, so that in [[tensor product]] notation <math>\mathcal{C}</math> writes
:<math>
\mathcal{C}=\sum_{j=1}^\infty \lambda_j \varphi_j\otimes\varphi_j.
</math>
Moreover, since <math>\mathcal Cf</math> is continuous for all <math>f\in H</math>, all the <math>\varphi_j</math> are continuous.  [[Mercer's theorem]] then states that
:<math>
\sup_{s,t\in [0,1]} \left|\Sigma(s,t) - \sum_{j=1}^K \lambda_j \varphi_j(s)\varphi_j(t)\right|\to0,\qquad K\to\infty.
</math>
Finally, under the extra assumption that <math>X</math> has continuous sample paths, namely that with probability one, the random function <math>X:[0,1]\to\mathbb R</math> is continuous, the Karhunen-Loève expansion above holds for <math>X</math> and the Hilbert space machinery can be subsequently applied.  Continuity of sample paths can be shown using [[Kolmogorov continuity theorem]].

== Functional data designs ==
Functional data are considered as realizations of a [[stochastic process]] <math>X(t),\ t\in[0,1]</math> that is an <math>L^2</math> process on a bounded and closed interval <math>[0,1]</math> with mean function <math>\mu(t)=\mathbb{E}(X(t))</math> and covariance function <math>\Sigma(s,t)=\textrm{Cov}(X(s),X(t))</math>. The realizations of the process for the i-th subject is <math>X_i(\cdot)</math>, and the sample is assumed to consist of <math>n</math> independent subjects. The sampling schedule may vary across subjects, denoted as <math>T_{i1},..., T_{iN_i}</math> for the i-th subject. The corresponding i-th observation is denoted as <math>\textbf{X}_i = (X_{i1},..., X_{iN_i}) </math>, where <math>X_{ij} = X_i(T_{ij})</math>. In addition, the measurement of <math>X_{ij} </math> is assumed to have random noise <math>\epsilon_{ij}</math> with <math>\mathbb{E}(\epsilon_{ij})=0</math> and <math>\textrm{Var}(\epsilon_{ij})=\sigma^2_{ij}</math>, which are independent across <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>.

=== 1. Fully observed functions without noise at arbitrarily dense grid ===
Measurements <math>
Y_{it}=X_i(t)
</math> available for all <math>
t\in \mathcal{I},\, i=1,\ldots,n
</math>

Often unrealistic but mathematically convenient.

Real life example: Tecator spectral data.<ref name=":7"/>

=== 2. Densely sampled functions with noisy measurements (dense design) ===
Measurements <math>
Y_{ij}=X_i(T_{ij}) + \varepsilon_{ij}
</math>, where <math>
T_{ij}
</math> are recorded on a regular grid,

<math>
T_{i1},\ldots,T_{iN_i}
</math>, and <math>
N_{i}\rarr\infty
</math> applies to typical functional data.

Real life example: [https://rdrr.io/cran/fda/man/growth.html#heading-0 Berkeley Growth Study Data] and [https://www.marketwatch.com/investing/stock/live Stock data]

=== 3. Sparsely sampled functions with noisy measurements (longitudinal data)  ===
Measurements <math>
Y_{ij}=X_i(T_{ij}) + \varepsilon_{ij}
</math>, where <math>
T_{ij}
</math> are random times and their number <math>
N_{i}
</math> per subject is random and finite.

Real life example: CD4 [[count data]] for AIDS patients.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Shi|first1=M|last2=Weiss|first2=RE|last3=Taylor|first3=JMG.|date=1996|title=An analysis of paediatric CD4 counts for acquired immune deficiency syndrome using flexible random curves|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series C (Applied Statistics)|volume=45|issue=2|pages=151–163}}</ref>

==Functional principal component analysis==

[[Functional principal component analysis]] (FPCA) is the most prevalent tool in FDA, partly because FPCA facilitates [[Dimensionality reduction|dimension reduction]] of the inherently infinite-dimensional functional data to finite-dimensional random vector of scores. More specifically, [[Dimensionality reduction|dimension reduction]] is achieved by expanding the underlying observed random trajectories <math>X_i(t)</math> in a functional basis consisting of the eigenfunctions of the covariance operator on <math>X</math>. Consider the covariance operator <math>\mathcal{C}: L^2[0,1] \rightarrow L^2[0,1]</math> as in ({{EquationNote|1}}), which is a [[compact operator on Hilbert space]].  

By [[Mercer's theorem]], the kernel function of <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, i.e., the covariance function <math>\Sigma (\cdot, \cdot)</math>, has spectral decomposition <math>\Sigma(s,t)=\sum^{\infty}_{k=1}\lambda_k\varphi_k(s)\varphi_k(t)</math>, where the series convergence is absolute and uniform, and <math>\lambda_k</math> are real-valued nonnegative eigenvalues in descending order with the corresponding orthonormal eigenfunctions <math>\varphi_k(t)</math> . By the [[Karhunen–Loève theorem]], the FPCA expansion of an underlying random trajectory is <math>X_i(t) =\mu(t)+\sum^{\infty}_{k=1} A_{ik}\varphi_k(t)</math>, where <math>A_{ik}=\int_0^1(X_i(t)-\mu(t))\varphi_k(t)dt</math> are the functional principal components (FPCs), sometimes referred to as scores. 

The Karhunen–Loève expansion facilitates [[Dimensionality reduction|dimension reduction]] in the sense that the partial sum converges uniformly, i.e., <math display=block>\lim_{K \rightarrow \infty} \sup_{t\in[0,1]} \mathbb{E}[X_i(t)-\mu(t)-\sum^{K}_{k=1}A_{ik}\varphi_k(t)]^2 \rightarrow 0</math> 
and thus the partial sum with a large enough <math>K</math> yields a good approximation to the infinite sum. Thereby, the information in <math>X_i</math> is reduced from infinite dimensional to a <math>K</math>-dimensional vector <math>A_i=(A_{i1},...,A_{iK})</math> with the approximated process： 
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">X_i^{(K)}(t) =\mu(t)+\sum^{K}_{k=1} A_{ik}\varphi_k(t)</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}Other popular bases include [[Spline (mathematics)|spline]], [[Fourier series]] and wavelet bases. Important applications of FPCA include the [[modes of variation]] and functional [[principal component regression]].

==Functional linear regression models==
[[Functional regression|Functional linear models]] can be viewed as an extension of the traditional [[Linear regression|multivariate linear models]] that associates vector responses with vector covariates. The traditional linear model with scalar response <math>Y\in\mathbb{R}</math> and vector covariate <math>X\in\mathbb{R}^p</math> can be expressed as 
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">Y = \beta_0 + \langle X,\beta\rangle + \varepsilon=\beta_0+X_1 \beta_1 + \dots +  X_p \beta_p + \varepsilon,</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}} 
where <math>\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle</math> denotes the [[Inner product space|inner product]] in [[Euclidean space]], <math>\beta_0\in\mathbb{R}</math> and <math>\beta\in\mathbb{R}^p</math> denote the regression coefficients, and <math>\varepsilon</math> is a zero [[Expected value|mean]] finite [[variance]] random error (noise). Functional linear models can be divided into two types based on the responses.

===Functional regression models with scalar response===
Replacing the vector covariate <math>X</math> and the coefficient vector <math>\beta</math> in model ({{EquationNote|3}}) by a centered functional covariate <math>X^c(t) = X(t) - \mu(t)</math> and coefficient function <math>\beta = \beta(t)</math> for <math>t \in [0,1]</math> and replacing the inner product in Euclidean space by that in [[Hilbert space]] [[Lp space|<math>L^2</math>]], one arrives at the functional linear model
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">Y = \beta_0 + \langle X^c, \beta\rangle +\varepsilon = \beta_0 + \int_0^1 X^c(t)\beta(t)\,dt + \varepsilon.</math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}
The simple functional linear model ({{EquationNote|4}}) can be extended to multiple functional covariates, <math>\{X_j\}_{j=1}^p</math>, also including additional vector covariates <math>Z = (Z_1, \cdots,Z_q)</math>, where <math>Z_1=1</math>, by
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">Y = \langle Z,\theta\rangle+ \sum_{j=1}^p \int_0^1 X_j^c(t) \beta_j(t) \,dt + \varepsilon,</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}
where <math>\theta\in \mathbb{R^q}</math> is regression coefficient for <math>Z</math>, the domain of <math>X_j</math> is <math>[0,1]</math>, <math>X^c_j</math> is the centered functional covariate given by <math>X_j^c(t) = X_j(t) - \mu_j(t)</math>, and <math>\beta_j</math> is regression coefficient function for <math>X_j^c </math>, for <math>j=1,\ldots,p</math>. Models ({{EquationNote|4}}) and ({{EquationNote|5}}) have been studied extensively.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hilgert|first1=N|last2=Mas|first2=A|last3=Verzelen|first3=N.|date=2013|title=Minimax adaptive tests for the functional linear model|url=|journal=Annals of Statistics|volume=41|issue=2|pages=838–869|doi=10.1214/13-AOS1093|s2cid=13119710|arxiv=1206.1194}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kong|first1=D|last2=Xue|first2=K|last3=Yao|first3=F|last4=Zhang|first4=HH.|date=2016|title=Partially functional linear regression in high dimensions|url=|journal=Biometrika|volume=103|issue=1|pages=147–159|doi=10.1093/biomet/asv062}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Horváth|first1=L|title=Inference for functional data with applications|last2=Kokoszka|first2=P.|date=2012|publisher=Springer-Verlag|series=Springer Series in Statistics}}</ref>

===Functional regression models with functional response===
Consider a functional response <math>Y(s)</math> on <math>[0,1]</math> and multiple functional covariates <math>X_j(t)</math>, <math>t\in [0,1]</math>, <math>j=1,\ldots,p</math>. Two major models have been considered in this setup.<ref name="wang:162">{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=JL|last2=Chiou|first2=JM|last3=Müller|first3=HG.|date=2016|title=Functional data analysis|journal=Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application|volume=3|issue=1|pages=257–295|doi=10.1146/annurev-statistics-041715-033624|bibcode=2016AnRSA...3..257W|s2cid=13709250 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/895750|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":7"/> One of these two models, generally referred to as functional linear model (FLM), can be written as:
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">Y(s) = \alpha_0(s) + \sum^p_{j=1} \int_0^1\alpha_j(s,t) X^c_j (t)\,dt + \varepsilon(s),\ \text{for}\ s\in[0,1]</math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
where <math>\alpha_0(s)</math> is the functional intercept, for <math>j=1,\ldots,p</math> , <math>X_j^c(t)=X_j(t) - \mu_j(t)</math> is a centered functional covariate on <math>[0,1]</math>, <math>\alpha_j(s,t)</math> is the corresponding functional slopes with same domain, respectively, and <math>\varepsilon(s)</math> is usually a random process with mean zero and finite variance.<ref name="wang:162"/> In this case, at any given time <math>s\in[0,1]</math>, the value of <math>Y</math>, i.e., <math>Y(s)</math>, depends on the entire trajectories of <math>\{X_j(t)\}^p_{j=1}</math>. Model ({{EquationNote|6}}) has been studied extensively.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ramsay|first1=JO|last2=Dalzell|first2=CJ.|date=1991|title=Some tools for functional data analysis|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B (Methodological)|volume=53|issue=3|pages=539–561|doi=10.1111/j.2517-6161.1991.tb01844.x|s2cid=118960346 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Malfait|first1=N|last2=Ramsay|first2=JO.|date=2003|title=The historical functional linear model|journal=The Canadian Journal of Statistics|volume=31|issue=2|pages=115–128|doi=10.2307/3316063|jstor=3316063|s2cid=55092204}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=He|first1=G|last2=Müller|first2=HG|last3=Wang|first3=JL.|date=2003|title=Functional canonical analysis for square integrable stochastic processes|journal=Journal of Multivariate Analysis|volume=85|issue=1|pages=54–77|doi=10.1016/S0047-259X(02)00056-8}}</ref><ref name=":5"/><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=He|first1=G|last2=Müller|first2=HG|last3=Wang|first3=JL|last4=Yang|first4=WJ.|date=2010|title=Functional linear regression via canonical analysis|journal=Journal of Multivariate Analysis|volume=16|issue=3|pages=705–729|doi=10.3150/09-BEJ228|arxiv=1102.5212|s2cid=17843044}}</ref>

==== Function-on-scalar regression ====
In particular, taking <math>X_j(\cdot)</math> as a constant function yields a special case of model ({{EquationNote|6}})<math display="block">Y(s) = \alpha_0(s)+\sum_{j=1}^p X_j \alpha_j(s) + \varepsilon(s),\ \text{for}\ s\in[0,1],</math>which is a functional linear model with functional responses and scalar covariates.

==== Concurrent regression models ====
This model is given by
{{NumBlk|::|<math display="block">Y(s) = \beta_0(s) + \sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j(s)X_j(s)+\varepsilon(s),\ \text{for}\ s\in[0,1],</math>|{{EquationRef|7}}}}
where <math>X_1,\ldots,X_p</math> are functional covariates on <math>[0,1]</math>, <math>\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p</math> are the coefficient functions defined on the same interval and <math>\varepsilon(s)</math> is usually assumed to be a random process with mean zero and finite variance.<ref name="wang:162"/> This model assumes that the value of <math>Y(s)</math> depends on the current value of <math>\{X_j(s)\}^p_{j=1}</math> only and not the history <math>\{X_j(t):t\le s\}^p_{j=1}</math> or future value. Hence, it is a "concurrent regression model", which is also referred as "varying-coefficient" model. Further, various estimation methods have been proposed.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fan|first1=J|last2=Zhang|first2=W.|date=1999|title=Statistical estimation in varying coefficient models|journal=The Annals of Statistics|volume=27|issue=5|pages=1491–1518|doi=10.1214/aos/1017939139|s2cid=16758288|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=CO|last2=Yu|first2=KF.|date=2002|title=Nonparametric varying-coefficient models for the analysis of longitudinal data|journal=International Statistical Review|volume=70|issue=3|pages=373–393|doi=10.1111/j.1751-5823.2002.tb00176.x|s2cid=122007787}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Huang|first1=JZ|last2=Wu|first2=CO|last3=Zhou|first3=L.|date=2002|title=Varying-coefficient models and basis function approximations for the analysis of repeated measurements|journal=Biometrika|volume=89|issue=1|pages=111–128|doi=10.1093/biomet/89.1.111}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Huang|first1=JZ|last2=Wu|first2=CO|last3=Zhou|first3=L.|date=2004|title=Polynomial spline estimation and inference for varying coefficient models with longitudinal data|journal=Statistica Sinica|volume=14|issue=3|pages=763–788}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Şentürk|first1=D|last2=Müller|first2=HG.|date=2010|title=Functional varying coefficient models for longitudinal data|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=105|issue=491|pages=1256–1264|doi=10.1198/jasa.2010.tm09228|s2cid=14296231}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Eggermont|first1=PPB|last2=Eubank|first2=RL|last3=LaRiccia|first3=VN.|date=2010|title=Convergence rates for smoothing spline estimators in varying coefficient models|journal=Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference|volume=140|issue=2|pages=369–381|doi=10.1016/j.jspi.2009.06.017}}</ref>

== Functional nonlinear regression models ==
Direct nonlinear extensions of the classical functional linear regression models (FLMs) still involve a linear predictor, but combine it with a nonlinear link function, analogous to the idea of [[generalized linear model]] from the conventional linear model. Developments towards fully nonparametric regression models for functional data encounter problems such as [[curse of dimensionality]]. In order to bypass the "curse" and the metric selection problem, we are motivated to consider nonlinear functional regression models, which are subject to some structural constraints but do not overly infringe flexibility. One desires models that retain polynomial rates of convergence, while being more flexible than, say, functional linear models. Such models are particularly useful when diagnostics for the functional linear model indicate lack of fit, which is often encountered in real life situations.  In particular, functional polynomial models, functional [[Semiparametric regression#Index models|single and multiple index models]] and functional [[additive model]]s are three special cases of functional [[nonlinear regression]] models.

=== Functional polynomial regression models ===
Functional polynomial regression models may be viewed as a natural extension of the Functional Linear Models (FLMs) with scalar responses, analogous to extending linear regression model  to [[polynomial regression]] model. For a scalar response <math>Y</math> and a functional covariate <math>X(\cdot)</math> with domain <math>[0,1]</math> and the corresponding centered predictor processes <math>X^c</math>, the simplest and the most prominent member in the family of functional polynomial regression models is the quadratic functional regression<ref name="yao:10">Yao, F; Müller, HG. (2010). "Functional quadratic regression". ''Biometrika''. '''97''' (1):49–64.</ref> given as follows,<math display="block">\mathbb{E}(Y|X) = \alpha + \int_0^1\beta(t)X^c(t)\,dt + \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \gamma(s,t) X^c(s)X^c(t) \,ds\,dt </math>where <math>X^c(\cdot) = X(\cdot) - \mathbb{E}(X(\cdot))</math> is the centered functional covariate, <math>\alpha</math> is a scalar coefficient, <math>\beta(\cdot)</math> and <math>\gamma(\cdot,\cdot)</math> are coefficient functions with domains <math>[0,1]</math> and <math>[0,1]\times[0,1]</math>, respectively. In addition to the parameter function β that the above functional quadratic regression model shares with the FLM, it also features a parameter surface γ. By analogy to FLMs with scalar responses, estimation of functional polynomial models can be obtained through expanding both the centered covariate <math>X^c</math> and the coefficient functions <math>\beta</math> and <math>\gamma</math> in an orthonormal basis.<ref name="yao:10" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Horváth|first1=L|last2=Reeder|first2=R.|date=2013|title=A test of significance in functional quadratic regression|journal=Bernoulli|volume=19|issue=5A|pages=2120–2151|doi=10.3150/12-BEJ446|s2cid=88512527|doi-access=free|arxiv=1105.0014}}</ref>

=== Functional single and multiple index models ===

A functional multiple index model is given as below, with symbols having their usual meanings as formerly described,<math display="block"> \mathbb{E}(Y|X) = g\left(\int_0^1X^c(t) \beta_1(t)\,dt, \ldots, \int_0^1X^c(t) \beta_p(t)\,dt \right) </math>Here g represents an (unknown) general smooth function defined on a p-dimensional domain. The case  <math>p=1</math> yields a functional single index model while multiple index models correspond to the case  <math>p>1</math>. However, for <math>p>1</math>, this model is problematic due to [[curse of dimensionality]]. With <math>p>1</math> and relatively small sample sizes, the estimator given by this model often has large variance.<ref name="chen:11">Chen, D; Hall, P; Müller HG. (2011). "Single and multiple index functional regression models with nonparametric link". ''The Annals of Statistics''. '''39''' (3):1720–1747.</ref><ref>Jiang, CR; Wang JL. (2011). "Functional single index models for longitudinal data". ''he Annals of Statistics''. '''39''' (1):362–388.</ref>

=== Functional additive models (FAMs) ===
For a given orthonormal basis <math>\{\phi_k\}_{k=1}^\infty</math> on <math>L^2[0,1]</math>, we can expand <math>X^c(t) =\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k \phi_k(t)</math> on the domain <math>[0,1]</math>.

A functional linear model with scalar responses (see ({{EquationNote|3}})) can thus be written as follows,<math display="block">\mathbb{E}(Y|X)=\mathbb{E}(Y) + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \beta_k x_k.</math>One form of FAMs is obtained by replacing the linear function of <math>x_k</math> in the above expression ( i.e., <math>\beta_k x_k</math>) by a general smooth function <math>f_k</math>, analogous to the extension of multiple linear regression models to additive models and is expressed as,<math display="block">\mathbb{E}(Y|X)=\mathbb{E}(Y) + \sum_{k=1}^\infty f_k(x_k),</math>where <math>f_k</math> satisfies <math>\mathbb{E}(f_k(x_k))=0</math> for <math>k\in\mathbb{N}</math>.<ref name="wang:162"/><ref name=":7" /> This constraint on the general smooth functions <math>f_k</math> ensures identifiability in the sense that the estimates of these additive component functions do not interfere with that of the intercept term <math>\mathbb{E}(Y)</math>. Another form of FAM is the continuously additive model,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Müller HG; Wu Y; Yao|first=F.|date=2013|title=Continuously additive models for nonlinear functional regression|journal=Biometrika|volume=100|issue=3|pages=607–622|doi=10.1093/biomet/ast004}}</ref> expressed as,<math display="block">\mathbb{E}(Y|X) = \mathbb{E}(Y) + \int_0^1 g(t,X(t)) dt</math>for a bivariate smooth additive surface <math>g:[0,1]\times\mathbb{R} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> which is required to satisfy <math>\mathbb{E}[g(t,X(t))]=0</math> for all <math>t\in[0,1]</math>, in order to ensure identifiability.

=== Generalized functional linear model ===
An obvious and direct extension of FLMs with scalar responses (see ({{EquationNote|3}})) is to add a link function leading to a [[generalized functional linear model]] (GFLM)<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Müller HG; Stadmüller|first=U.|date=2005|title=Generalized Functional Linear Models|journal=The Annals of Statistics|volume=33|issue=2|pages=774–805|doi=10.1214/009053604000001156|arxiv=math/0505638}}</ref> in analogy to the [[generalized linear model]] (GLM). The three components of the GFLM are:

# [[Linear predictor function|Linear predictor]] <math>\eta = \beta_0 + \int_0^1 X^c(t)\beta(t)\,dt</math>;  [systematic component]
# [[Variance function]] <math>\text{Var}(Y|X) = V(\mu)</math>, where <math>\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y|X)</math> is the [[Conditional expectation|conditional mean]];  [random component]
# [[Link function]] <math>g</math> connecting the conditional mean <math>\mu</math> and the linear predictor <math>\eta</math> through <math>\mu=g(\eta)</math>.  [systematic component]

== Clustering and classification of functional data ==
For vector-valued multivariate data, [[K-means clustering|k-means partitioning methods]] and [[hierarchical clustering]] are two main approaches. These classical clustering concepts for vector-valued multivariate data have been extended to functional data. For clustering of functional data, k-means clustering methods are more popular than hierarchical clustering methods. For k-means clustering on functional data, mean functions are usually regarded as the cluster centers. Covariance structures have also been taken into consideration.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chiou|first1=JM|last2=Li|first2=PL.|date=2007|title=Functional clustering and identifying substructures of longitudinal data|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B (Statistical Methodology)|volume=69|issue=4|pages=679–699|doi=10.1111/j.1467-9868.2007.00605.x|s2cid=120883171|doi-access=free}}</ref> Besides k-means type clustering, functional clustering<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Banfield|first1=JD|last2=Raftery|first2=AE.|date=1993|title=Model-based Gaussian and non-Gaussian clustering|journal=Biometrics|volume=49|issue=3|pages=803–821|doi=10.2307/2532201|jstor=2532201}}</ref> based on [[mixture model]]s is also widely used in clustering vector-valued multivariate data and has been extended to functional data clustering.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=James|first1=GM|last2=Sugar|first2=CA.|date=2003|title=Clustering for sparsely sampled functional data|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=98|issue=462|pages=397–408|doi=10.1198/016214503000189|s2cid=9487422}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jacques|first1=J|last2=Preda|first2=C.|date=2013|title=Funclust: A curves clustering method using functional random variables density approximation|journal=Neurocomputing|volume=112|pages=164–171|doi=10.1016/j.neucom.2012.11.042|s2cid=33591208|url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00628247v2/file/Paper-Funclust-V2-versionHAL.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jacques|first1=J|last2=Preda|first2=C.|date=2014|title=Model-based clustering for multivariate functional data|journal=Computational Statistics & Data expression data|journal=Computational Statistics & Data Analysis|volume=71|issue=C|pages=14–29|doi=10.1016/j.csda.2013.04.001}}</ref><ref>{{Cite Functional classification assigns a group membership to a new data object either based on functional regression or functional discriminant analysis. Functional data classification methods based on functional regression models use class levels as responses and the observed functional data and other covariates as predictors. For regression based functional classification models, functional generalized linear models or more specifically, functional binary regression, such as functional [[logistic regression]] for binary responses, are commonly used classification approaches. More generally, the generalized functional linear regression model based on the [[Functional principal component analysis|FPCA approach]] is used.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Leng|first1=X|last2=Müller|first2=HG.|date=2006|title=Classification using functional data analysis for temporal gene expression data|journal=Bioinformatics|volume=22|issue=1|pages=68–76|doi=10.1093/bioinformatics/bti742|pmid=16257986|doi-access=free|url=http://bioinformatics.oxfordjournals.org/content/early/2005/10/27/bioinformatics.bti742.full.pdf}}</ref> Functional Linear Discriminant Analysis (FLDA) has also been considered as a classification method for functional data.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=James|first1=GM|last2=Hastie|first2=TJ.|date=2001|title=Functional linear discriminant analysis for irregularly sampled curves|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical ==Time warping==

=== Motivations ===
[[File:Motivation-timewarping-sim.png|thumb|alt=Illustration of the motivation of time warping in the sense of capturing cross-sectional mean.|500px|Structures in cross-sectional mean destroyed if time variation is ignored. On the contrary, structures in cross-sectional mean is well-captured after restoring time variation.]]

In addition to amplitude variation,<ref name="wang:16">{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=JL|last2=Chiou|first2=JM|last3=Müller|first3=HG.|date=2016|title=Functional Data Analysis|journal=Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application|volume=3|issue=1|pages=257–295|doi=10.1146/annurev-statistics-041715-033624|bibcode=2016AnRSA...3..257W|s2cid=13709250 |url=https://zenodo.org/record/895750|doi-access=free}}</ref> time variation may also be assumed to present in functional data. Time variation occurs when the subject-specific timing of certain events of interest varies among subjects. One classical example is the [https://rdrr.io/cran/fda/man/growth.html#heading-0 Berkeley Growth Study Data],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gasser|first1=T|last2=Müller|first2=HG|last3=Kohler|first3=W|last4=Molinari|first4=L|last5=Prader|first5=A.|date=1984|title=Nonparametric regression analysis of growth curves|journal=The Annals of Statistics|volume=12|issue=1|pages=210–229|doi=}}</ref> where the amplitude variation is the growth rate and the time variation explains the difference in children's biological age at which the pubertal and the pre-pubertal growth spurt occurred. In the presence of time variation, the cross-sectional mean function may not be an efficient estimate as peaks and troughs are located randomly and thus meaningful signals may be distorted or hidden.

Time warping, also known as curve registration,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ramsay|first1=JO|last2=Li|first2=X.|date=1998|title=Curve registration|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B|volume=60|issue=2|pages=351–363|doi=10.1111/1467-9868.00129|s2cid=17175587|doi-access=free}}</ref> curve alignment or time synchronization, aims to identify and separate amplitude variation and time variation. If both time and amplitude variation are present, then the observed functional data <math>Y_i</math> can be modeled as <math>Y_i(t)=X_i[h_i^{-1}(t)], t\in [0,1]</math>, where <math>X_i\overset{iid}{\sim}X</math> is a latent amplitude function and <math>h_i\overset{iid}{\sim} h</math> is a latent time warping function that corresponds to a cumulative distribution function. The time warping functions <math>h</math> are assumed to be invertible and to satisfy <math>\mathbb{E}(h^{-1}(t))=t</math>.

The simplest case of a family of warping functions to specify phase variation is linear transformation, that is <math>h(t)=\delta+\gamma t</math>, which warps the time of an underlying template function by subjected-specific shift and scale. More general class of warping functions includes [[diffeomorphism]]s of the domain to itself, that is, loosely speaking, a class of invertible functions that maps the compact domain to itself such that both the function and its inverse are smooth. The set of linear transformation is contained in the set of [[diffeomorphism]]s.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last1=Marron|first1=JS|last2=Ramsay|first2=JO|last3=Sangalli|first3=LM|last4=Srivastava|first4=A|date=2015|title=Functional data analysis of amplitude and phase variation|journal=Statistical Science|volume=30|issue=4|pages=468–484|doi=10.1214/15-STS524|arxiv=1512.03216|s2cid=55849758}}</ref> One challenge in time warping is identifiability of amplitude and phase variation. Specific assumptions are required to break this non-identifiability.

=== Methods ===
Earlier approaches include [[dynamic time warping]] (DTW) used for applications such as [[speech recognition]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sakoe|first1=H|last2=Chiba|first2=S.|date=1978|title=Dynamic programming algorithm optimization for spoken word recognition|journal=IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing|volume=26|pages=43–49|doi=10.1109/TASSP.1978.1163055|s2cid=17900407}}</ref> Another traditional method for time warping is landmark registration,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kneip|first1=A|last2=Gasser|first2=T|date=1992|title=Statistical tools to analyze data representing a sample of curves|journal=Annals of Statistics|volume=20|issue=3|pages=1266–1305|doi=10.1214/aos/1176348769|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gasser|first1=T|last2=Kneip|first2=A|date=1995|title=Searching for structure in curve sample|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=90|issue=432|pages=1179–1188|doi=}}</ref> which aligns special features such as peak locations to an average location. Other relevant warping methods include pairwise warping,<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Tang|first1=R|last2=Müller|first2=HG.|date=2008|title=Pairwise curve synchronization for functional data|journal=Biometrika|volume=95|issue=4|pages=875–889|doi=10.1093/biomet/asn047}}</ref> registration using  <math>\mathcal{L}^2</math> distance<ref name=":6" /> and elastic warping.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Anirudh|first1=R|last2=Turaga|first2=P|last3=Su|first3=J|last4=Srivastava|first4=A|year=2015|title=Elastic functional coding of human actions: From vector-fields to latent variables|journal=Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition|pages=3147–3155|arxiv=}}</ref>

====Dynamic time warping====
The template function is determined through an iteration process, starting from cross-sectional mean, performing registration and recalculating the cross-sectional mean for the warped curves, expecting convergence after a few iterations. DTW minimizes a cost function through dynamic programming. Problems of non-smooth differentiable warps or greedy computation in DTW can be resolved by adding a regularization term to the cost function.

====Landmark registration====
Landmark registration (or feature alignment) assumes well-expressed features are present in all sample curves and uses the location of such features as a gold-standard. Special features such as peak or trough locations in functions or derivatives are aligned to their average locations on the template function.<ref name=":6" /> Then the warping function is introduced through a smooth transformation from the average location to the subject-specific locations. A problem of landmark registration is that the features may be missing or hard to identify due to the noise in the data.

== Extensions ==
So far we considered scalar valued stochastic process, <math>
\{X(t)\}_{t\in \mathcal T}
</math>, defined on one dimensional time domain.

=== Multidimensional domain of <math>X(\cdot)</math> ===
The domain of <math>
X(\cdot)
</math> can be in <math>
R^p
</math>, for example the data could be a sample of random surfaces.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Dubey|first1=P|last2=Müller|first2=HG|date=2021|title=Modeling Time-Varying Random Objects and Dynamic Networks|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=117|issue=540|pages=2252–2267|doi=10.1080/01621459.2021.1917416|arxiv=2104.04628|s2cid=233210300}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pigoli|first1=D|last2=Hadjipantelis|first2=PZ|last3=Coleman|first3=JS|last4=Aston|first4=JAD|date=2017|title=The statistical analysis of acoustic phonetic data: exploring differences between spoken Romance languages|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series C (Applied Statistics)|volume=67|issue=5|pages=1130–1145}}</ref>

=== Multivariate stochastic process ===
The range set of the stochastic process may be extended from <math>
R
</math> to <math>
R^p
</math><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Happ|first1=C|last2=Greven|first2=S|date=2018|title=Multivariate Functional Principal Component Analysis for Data Observed on Different (Dimensional) Domains|journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association|volume=113|issue=522|pages=649–659|doi=10.1080/01621459.2016.1273115|s2cid=88521295|arxiv=1509.02029}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chiou|first1=JM|last2=Yang|first2=YF|last3=Chen|first3=YT|date=2014|title=Multivariate functional principal component analysis: a normalization approach|journal=Statistica Sinica|volume=24|pages=1571–1596}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Carroll|first1=C|last2=Müller|first2=HG|last3=Kneip|first3=A|date=2021|title=Cross-component registration for multivariate functional data, with application to growth curves|journal=Biometrics|volume=77|issue=3|pages=839–851|doi=10.1111/biom.13340|arxiv=1811.01429|s2cid=220687157}}</ref> and further to nonlinear manifolds,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dai|first1=X|last2=Müller|first2=HG|date=2018|title=Principal component analysis for functional data on Riemannian manifolds and spheres|journal=The Annals of Statistics|volume=46|issue=6B|pages=3334–3361|doi=10.1214/17-AOS1660|s2cid=13671221|arxiv=1705.06226}}</ref> Hilbert spaces<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=K|last2=Delicado|first2=P|last3=Müller|first3=HG|date=2017|title=Modelling function-valued stochastic processes, with applications to fertility dynamics|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B (Statistical Methodology)|volume=79|issue=1|pages=177–196|doi=10.1111/rssb.12160|hdl=2117/126653|s2cid=13719492|hdl-access=free}}</ref> and eventually to metric spaces.<ref name=":3" />
